I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

It has been revealed that these popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

Sources indicate that the most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

Sources indicate that one of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

In a recent development, the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Industry observers note that another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

In a recent development, financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive strategy for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

Recent findings suggest that while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

In a recent development, financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable strategy to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

Industry observers note that moneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

Recent findings suggest that one of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

In a recent development, the teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

In a recent development, moneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

Sources indicate that moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

According to recent reports, I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a strategy that fit my unique situation and goals.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

In a recent development, for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

According to recent reports, if you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most key thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one organization usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies.
  • That happens because the discount comes off one firm’s own prices.
  • Some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one organization usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies. Before you switch or renew, get the bundled price and the best separate quotes for the same coverage, and buy whichever total is lower.

That happens because the discount comes off one firm’s own prices. The Insurance Information Institute indicates homeowners insurance for the same house can cost hundreds of dollars more at one insurer than at another.

Some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute notes. It also tells buyers to make sure the bundle costs less than buying each policy from a different company.

Industry observers note that say a family asks three insurers to quote the same coverage. The best bundle comes to $3,100 a year, and the cheapest home and car policies from two different companies total $2,850, so buying separately saves $250 a year. Next door, the best bundle costs $600 less than the cheapest separate policies, so the neighbors bundle.

Recent findings suggest that home, condo, and renters policies usually count toward the discount alongside a car policy. Some insurers also count a life insurance policy or an umbrella policy, which adds liability coverage on top of your home and car policies. Bundling also means one firm to call when a storm damages your roof and your car, and some insurers then charge one deductible instead of two. Treat those perks as a tiebreaker when the totals are close.

Industry observers note that separate quotes matter most when your car or your home is hard to insure. A driver with recent speeding tickets may find the lowest car rate at one tech giant and the lowest home rate at another. A home insured through your state’s FAIR plan, the last-resort insurer for homes that private companies won’t cover, can’t be bundled at all, since the plan doesn’t sell car insurance.

According to recent reports, get every quote for the same coverage amounts, deductibles, and add-ons, from an agent or an online comparison tool. A quote with lower coverage amounts can look cheaper only because it pays less after a loss.

Before you split a bundle, ask your current insurer what the policy you’d keep will cost on its own, since dropping the other policy can end its discount.

Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again.
  • In a recent development, promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place.
  • The reward is often not the thing you buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again. Work out what sets yours off and what it gives you, then proposal a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward, and mark each day you follow it.

In a recent development, promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place. Each time the cue shows up, you still want the reward, and you have to talk yourself out of it again.

The reward is often not the thing you buy. Delivery after a rough day gives you a night off from cooking and some comfort. Late-night browsing on shopping sites gives you a distraction, and a lottery ticket gives you a few days of daydreaming about a win.

A cheaper routine can give you that comfort, distraction, or daydream, so you still get what you were after.

Track the habit for a week or two. Each time, note when and where it happens, how you feel, and what you get out of it. The time, place, or mood that keeps coming up is the cue, and the feeling it leaves you with is the reward.

Then set up a swap, a cheaper routine with a similar reward, before the cue comes back. Say two rough workdays a week end in a $30 delivery order, and a frozen dinner costs $7. Keep two in the freezer for those nights and call a friend on the walk home for the comfort. The dinner is plainer than takeout but still spares you the cooking. Those nights now cost about $60 a month instead of $260, a saving of about $200.

Industry observers note that take on one habit at a time. Mark each day you choose the swap on a calendar, and move what it saves into savings each week so you can watch the balance grow. A financial therapist can help with a habit that keeps returning despite a good swap.

Give the new routine time. In a University College London study, a new daily habit took 66 days on average to become automatic. Missing a single day had no lasting effect, but about half the volunteers didn’t do it often enough to form the habit. After a slip, run the swap again the next time the cue shows up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions.
  • A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count notes nothing about the hours the piece takes.
  • In a recent development, say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions. Time a few typical pieces from start to finish, multiply the hours by the hourly rate you need, and quote the total as a project fee. Charge more for specialist topics, rush deadlines, and contracts that buy all rights.

A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count notes nothing about the hours the piece takes.

In a recent development, say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour. Quote at least $450, which works out to 30 cents a word. A client offering 10 cents a word would pay $150 for the same 6 hours, or $25 an hour.

Thirty cents a word is in line with the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart, built from a survey of more than 1,100 editorial freelancers. Its median range for work-for-hire articles and essays, which the client owns outright, runs from 25 to 45 cents a word.

Sources indicate that start from the hourly rate you need, which is the yearly income you want plus your business costs and self-employment tax, divided by the hours you can bill clients for. Then time three typical pieces from first research to final revision, including interviews, client calls, and email. Multiply your average hours by that rate, and quote the result as a flat project fee. For a client who pays by the word, divide the fee by the word count to get the per-word rate to ask for.

Industry observers note that specialist knowledge, technical or regulated subjects like medicine, credentials such as a CPA license, and rush deadlines all justify a higher fee. In the same rate chart, median ranges for work-for-hire medical and technical writing start at $1 a word. Selling more rights should cost the client more. A contract that buys all rights, or makes the piece work for hire, leaves you nothing to resell or reprint, so price it above one that buys only the right to publish the piece first.

Over time, collect testimonials, quote each new client above the last, and win more clients directly, since no platform takes a share of what they pay.

Divide every offer by the hours the piece will take, and counter any that fall short of your hourly rate with your project fee.

Industry News: The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s.
  • Sources indicate that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival.
  • We're not in an official bear market, yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

Sources indicate that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

According to recent reports, so I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

It has been revealed that as the midterm elections showed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

As long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

But that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The upcoming car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

It has been revealed that if you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

If you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Industry observers note that lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

According to recent reports, retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

Sources indicate that but here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

Sources indicate that how do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

In a recent development, so how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

According to recent reports, according to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market highlights up about once every six years.

Sources indicate that in other words, if you proposal on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

According to recent reports, hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Industry observers note that two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

But here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

Industry observers note that my takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, plan on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

In a recent development, during a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

Recent findings suggest that during a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, new socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

Sources indicate that so you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

It has been revealed that with this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

It has been revealed that therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

It has been revealed that happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

Sources indicate that 1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

Recent findings suggest that 2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

Sources indicate that 5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

The market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

If your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your initiative has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paying off a non-medical collection helps only newer credit scores. FICO Score 9 and 10 and VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0 stop counting a collection once it’s paid, while paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 and older versions. Before you pay anything, get the collector’s terms in writing, including whether it will delete the account from your credit reports.

Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports. It stays seven years from the missed payment that started it, paid or not, unless it’s a medical collection, which the credit bureaus drop once it’s paid.

According to recent reports, FICO says its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance. VantageScore’s models have ignored paid collections since version 3.0 in 2013. Paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 or older versions.

That difference matters for a mortgage. The Federal Housing Finance Agency lets lenders selling loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac choose Classic FICO, an older model that still counts a paid collection, or VantageScore 4.0, which ignores it. Ask your lender which one it uses, and whether the loan requires collections paid off by closing.

Handle the collector in this order.

Sources indicate that say a collector agrees in writing to settle your $900 cable bill for $500. FICO Score 9 then treats the zero-balance account as paid and stops counting it, but the report lists it as settled, not paid in full. The $400 forgiven counts as taxable income unless an exception such as insolvency applies, with or without a Form 1099-C reporting it.

Pull your free weekly reports at AnnualCreditReport.com after you pay, and dispute the account with any bureau whose report doesn’t match the signed letter, sending a copy as proof.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most notable things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who right now draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

Industry observers note that but for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

In a recent development, those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

Recent findings suggest that that little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

Industry observers note that first let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

Recent findings suggest that when you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be significant enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re fresh to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

It has been revealed that what this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Sources indicate that now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a massive lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:.

In a recent development, so the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:.

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

Recent findings suggest that and of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

It has been revealed that the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a massive boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

In a recent development, sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

In a recent development, first of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Recent findings suggest that now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all challenges. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Opportunity Zone Funds Defer Capital Gains Tax – Tax-Free Growth Takes 10 Years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Put a capital gain into an opportunity zone fund only if you’d reinvest that money anyway and can leave it there for 10 years.
  • In a recent development, the 2025 tax law that made opportunity zones permanent set those terms, and they start on Jan.
  • After you sell stock, a business, or property at a gain, you have 180 days to put that gain into a qualified opportunity fund, which invests in designated low-income areas called opportunity zones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Put a capital gain into an opportunity zone fund only if you’d reinvest that money anyway and can leave it there for 10 years. For money invested from 2027, the tax on the gain is put off for five years and trimmed, not erased. The fund’s own growth goes tax-free only after a decade.

In a recent development, the 2025 tax law that made opportunity zones permanent set those terms, and they start on Jan. 1, 2027, when the Treasury’s upcoming zones take effect.

After you sell stock, a business, or property at a gain, you have 180 days to put that gain into a qualified opportunity fund, which invests in designated low-income areas called opportunity zones. The tax on the gain is deferred for five years. Then 10% of the gain goes untaxed, or 30% if the fund keeps at least 90% of its assets in rural zones. Hold the fund at least 10 years, and its growth is tax-free when you sell, though growth after its 30th year is taxed.

Say a fund at least holds its value, and you put a $200,000 gain from a 2027 stock sale into it. Your 2032 return reports $180,000 of that gain, and that tax comes due while the fund still holds your money. Sell after 10 years, in 2037 at the earliest, and the fund’s growth is tax-free.

The switch to the fresh rules makes timing matter. Gains already deferred under the old rules become taxable on Dec. 31, 2026, and IRS guidance bars rolling them into a new fund. A 2026 gain whose 180 days run into January 2027 can wait and go in under the new rules.

It has been revealed that only the gain qualifies, so any extra money you add counts as a separate investment with no tax break. Getting the full break also means leaving your money in projects in low-income areas for a decade, and the manager’s fees cut your return. The state securities regulators’ association warns that you could escape the tax and still lose your whole investment.

It has been revealed that so judge the fund as an investment first. Read what it will build and where, look up its manager and anyone selling it to you on FINRA’s BrokerCheck, and get every fee in writing.

Before you sign, ask whether you’d buy the fund with no tax break, and walk away if the answer is no.

#9867. Latest Update: Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

Latest Update: Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m a proponent of stealth wealth.
  • Sources indicate that stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades.
  • Industry observers note that so by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Sources indicate that stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend.

Industry observers note that so by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

In private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better. Here are three simple steps to follow:.

1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

Industry observers note that 2) Drive an old car. Driving a latest car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

According to recent reports, 3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

According to recent reports, once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

My parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

In a recent development, at the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 31-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

Then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

According to recent reports, and you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

Sources indicate that today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I stopped needing respect from everyone.

I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such conspicuous spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? We think to ourselves. But we’re missing something important.

Recent findings suggest that her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

This resonated with me as a minority who came to America for high school and faced various racist incidents. Racism is one of the deepest forms of disrespect because you're insulted just for being who you are. Respect, especially for elders, is a big part of Asian culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

Industry observers note that when you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

In a recent development, at 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

According to recent reports, then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

In a recent development, today, insults from random folks feel more like pinches instead of body blows. The passive income is doing its job as a shield.

As a dad now, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no massive deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

In a recent development, in that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the big deal?

In a recent development, yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

According to recent reports, reaching FIRE doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect.

Maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

Industry observers note that whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else. Know that there is an incredible joy of being a nobody so long as you have your finances in order.

In a recent development, for many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

That’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

Readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

In a recent development, stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

  • A syndication’s projected returns are the sponsor’s own forecast, and the sponsor collects fees whether or not they come true.
  • Sources indicate that A syndication pools money from passive investors, the limited partners, to buy one large property, such as an apartment complex, and borrows the rest of the price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you invest in a real estate syndication, vet the sponsor, not just its projected returns. Ask how its past deals did when rates jumped, how much of its own money is in this one, and whether the loan’s rate can rise with the market. Commit only money you can leave in for five to seven years.

A syndication’s projected returns are the sponsor’s own forecast, and the sponsor collects fees whether or not they come true.

Sources indicate that A syndication pools money from passive investors, the limited partners, to buy one large property, such as an apartment complex, and borrows the rest of the price. The sponsor runs it and typically sells after five to seven years. It earns an acquisition fee when it buys, an asset management fee each year, and a promote, often 20% to 30% of the profit above a set yearly return investors get first, called the preferred return. Only the promote depends on how investors do, so the sponsor’s skill and honesty matter more than the projections.

While rates were low, the syndicator Tides Equities bought apartments with floating-rate loans, whose interest rises with market rates. Its rate caps, which limit how high the rate can go, lasted only two or three years. When its first loans came due, rates had jumped, and Tides couldn’t afford new caps or a refinance, The Real Deal reported. Lenders foreclosed on some of its complexes, and anyone with $50,000 in one of those deals lost all of it.

Vet the sponsor yourself, even when a real estate investing platform lists the deal. Ask it to show you:.

Then check the deal. For a floating-rate loan, ask when the rate cap runs out and when the loan comes due. Compare the rents and sale price the sponsor assumes with what similar buildings rent and sell for now. Also find out whether the sponsor can make a capital call, a demand for more money, and what happens to investors who can’t pay.

Size your stake so you could leave it alone for seven years and still afford a capital call.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Keep every service receipt, fix a flaw only when the repair costs less than the next condition grade adds to the price, and sell before a redesign or a substantial scheduled service.

Kelley Blue Book values a used car at one of four condition grades, Excellent, Very Good, Good, or Fair, and each step down lowers the price. Half the cars it values land at Good.

Industry observers note that tires and paperwork help set the grade. Kelley Blue Book’s Very Good grade calls for matching tires with at least 75% of their tread and most service records, while Good asks for at least half the tread and some records.

So the grades tell you which repairs pay. Price the car in Kelley Blue Book’s value tool at its honest grade and one grade up, as a trade-in or a private sale, whichever you plan. Spend on dent repair, professional detailing, or latest tires only when the work costs less than the difference.

Until you sell, three habits protect the price:.

Brand and color are set for good, but fuel prices move. With fuel costs high in the third quarter of 2026, Cox Automotive found the wholesale prices dealers paid for large pickups and SUVs falling and those for EVs and smaller, fuel-efficient cars rising. So list a large pickup or SUV while gas is cheap.

Sell before a big scheduled service, such as replacing the timing belt, comes due, since a buyer will subtract its cost from the offer.

Automakers reveal a redesign months before it goes on sale, and the fresh version draws buyers from yours, so list your car before it arrives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, buying a home doesn’t take 20% down.
  • Most first-time buyers put down less than 20%.
  • Twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, buying a home doesn’t take 20% down. Many loans take as little as 3% or 3.5%, and VA loans for veterans and USDA loans for some rural buyers need no down payment. Set aside your cash for closing costs, moving, and emergencies first, then put down what’s left and weigh the mortgage insurance a smaller down payment adds.

Most first-time buyers put down less than 20%. Their median down payment was 9% in the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 buyer survey.

Twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying. A smaller down payment can also mean a higher interest rate. You can ask to drop PMI once you owe 80% of the home’s original value. Government-insured FHA loans keep their mortgage insurance for the life of the loan when you put down less than 10%.

Industry observers note that on a $350,000 home, 5% down is $17,500, against $70,000 for 20%. Freddie Mac estimates PMI at $30 to $70 a month per $100,000 borrowed, or roughly $100 to $230 a month on the $332,500 loan, a cost to weigh against the $52,500 you’d keep. Waiting costs something too. Home prices rose 2.4% in the year through August 2026, the Federal Housing Finance Agency reports. At that pace, if saving the other $52,500 takes three years, the same house will cost about $376,000, and 20% of it about $75,000. Buying sooner with less down avoids that rise, as long as your savings stay intact.

Start from the lowest down payment your loan allows, on a home that appraises for at least its price.

Recent findings suggest that then set aside closing costs, typically 2% to 5% of the price, money for moving and repairs, and an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential bills. Whatever is left goes toward the down payment, and down payment assistance programs can help you reach your loan’s minimum. Ask lenders to quote your monthly payment at 5% and 10% down.

PMI can come off later, but cash you put into the house comes back out only if you borrow against it or sell.

Compare the best mortgage lenders for a loan that fits the down payment you choose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jost Kobusch is back in Nepal, preparing for the fourth round of his Everest project. His long-term goal is to climb solo in winter, without oxygen, self-supported, and via the Lho La and the West Ridge.

According to recent reports, “If I am good at something, it’s planning,” the 34-year-old German told ExplorersWeb. In this case, his plan is to arrive at the mountain in the best shape possible, physically and mentally.

In a recent development, kobusch arrived in Kathmandu two weeks ago, together with friends Nicolas Scheidtweiler, Manuela Brummer, and photographer Alex Pichon. The group soon moved to Manang in the Annapurna region and began acclimatizing in the Chulu range.

Jost Kobusch (in yellow) scouts around Manang. Photo: Alex Pichon.

It has been revealed that the plan was to spend a few nights at altitude and traverse the four Chulu peaks, all above 6,000m. “[However,] expeditions rarely unfold exactly as expected,” Kobusch admitted.

Recent findings suggest that A member in the team felt exhausted after reaching the summit of the second peak, and the group abandoned the traverse there. “At least, we traversed from the summit of Chulu Far East (6,059m) to the top of Chulu East (6,444m) from the southeast,” Kobusch stated. He claims their line between the two peaks was newly introduced.

The line followed by Kobusch and his team up Chulu East. Photo: Alex Pichon.

In a recent development, their next strategy will be to climb a 7,000m peak in the area before Kobusch moves to the Khumbu in November. “I want to reach 8,000m, but on a different mountain than Everest, before the beginning of winter,” he mentioned.

He wants to be completely acclimatized by the time he starts working on Everest on December 22, the start of calendar winter. Kobusch will have two photographers in Base Camp, but he will climb alone.

Acclimatization in Manang, Photo: Alex Pichon.

“I need to be able to move efficiently, make good decisions when I’m tired, manage risk alone, and stay comfortable in an environment where very small mistakes can have very serious consequences,” Kobusch recently wrote on social media. He says that so far, all is going well. “I’m feeling good, I’ve done my homework, and I will start again on Everest better prepared than ever.”.

Kobusch has attempted winter Everest solo on three previous occasions, always via the Lho La and the West Ridge, thus avoiding venturing alone into the Khumbu Icefall.

In his first attempt in 2019-20, he reached the West Shoulder and pushed above 7,300m. On the second attempt in 2021-22, high winds didn’t let him go beyond 6,400m. He planned to try again the following year, but he caught dengue fever while training in Nepal and had to cancel.

Once recovered, he soloed Denali in February-March 2023. Everest had to wait one more year, this time due to a back injury. On the third attempt in 2024-25, he reached his highest point yet: 7,537m on December 27.

Kobusch’s highest point is shown with a green circle, and the Hornbein Couloir is the pink line on the 3D map by RealityMaps.

According to recent reports, “The chances of success are not particularly high,” he recently wrote. “If I had to put a number on it, I would say around 20%. But that does not make the attempt meaningless. If anything, it is part of what makes it interesting.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as executor, settle the estate in order: get the court’s authority, inventory everything, and pay valid debts, taxes, and costs from an estate account before you distribute anything. If you hand out inheritances first and the estate runs short, the IRS can hold you personally responsible for the tax it still owes.

Family members may press for their shares within weeks, long before it’s safe to pay them.

Recent findings suggest that federal taxes come first when an estate can’t pay all its debts, according to IRS Publication 559. An executor who pays heirs ahead of a tax debt they knew of, or should have known of, owes it personally, up to the amount paid out ahead of it.

Industry observers note that hire a probate lawyer if the estate can’t cover its debts or an heir contests the will. Skip the executor’s fee if you’re the only heir, since the fee is taxable income and an inheritance isn’t.

Say a daughter and her brother inherit their father’s estate in equal shares, and she’s the executor. Over nine months she pays $20,000 of his final bills and taxes from the estate’s $250,000, and only then splits the remaining $230,000, $115,000 each.

Send IRS Form 5495 right after you file the final returns. The IRS then has nine months to name any tax due, and paying it ends your personal liability for those taxes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a parent, I have two main concerns for my children.
  • Will they be able to earn a livable wage in a world where AI keeps eating entry-level jobs?
  • According to recent reports, the second concern is bigger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a parent, I have two main concerns for my children.

The first is economic stability. Will they be able to earn a livable wage in a world where AI keeps eating entry-level jobs? I question the time and money we spend educating our kids all the time. So I've been aggressively saving and investing for their future, just in case.

According to recent reports, the second concern is bigger. Will my children find love?

Industry observers note that A net worth target gets more achievable the more you save and the more time goes by. Compounding is boring, but it's reliable. If the direction is correct, sooner or later you will get there.

Finding a partner is far more amorphous. Our kids can work on their communication skills, fitness, charm, education, hygiene, empathy, and finances. But all of that merely improves their odds. There are no guarantees.

Which brings me to the strangest business story of 2026.

In late October, The Fresh York Times reported that U.S. officials concluded a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset. She is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center tech giant and Nvidia cloud partner that rents computing power to Chinese firms.

Recent findings suggest that surveillance of her reportedly revealed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. And no, they are not related. Huang is a common surname like Smith.

Recent findings suggest that the Financial Times then reported that a U.S. government memo described the relationship as romantic. Her alleged goal was to gather information on Jensen and advanced AI chips, and to nudge him to lobby for looser chip exports to China.

The allegations come from anonymous officials and haven't been tested publicly. Officials reportedly don't believe Jensen knew about any intelligence activity. Nvidia states his interactions with her were routine customer meetings. China denies the whole thing. House Republican committee chairs want a closed-door briefing on November 18.

Industry observers note that so nobody outside the room knows the full story, except that Jensen admitted to the affair and is no longer CEO as of November 23, 2026. The lessons about love and money are worth discussing regardless of how the facts shake out.

Jensen Huang is worth over $120 billion (once $170 billion). He runs a company worth about $4 trillion after the sell-off. He is the closest thing we have to a modern-day emperor, the face of the AI revolution, mobbed like a rock star everywhere he goes in Taiwan.

And yet, if the reporting is accurate, it still wasn't enough.

In a recent development, there's a line from Gemma Teller Morrow in the TV show, Sons of Anarchy: “Only men need to be loved, sweetheart. Women need to be wanted.”.

It's not entirely true. Everybody wants to be loved and desired to some degree. But the line points to something uncomfortable. No amount of money, applause, or leather jackets fills the need to feel admired by one specific person who seems to see you.

We all just want to be loved and accepted for who we are.

Here's the twist that makes this story sadder.

If U.S. officials are right, what may have felt like admiration was tradecraft. Attentiveness, respect, and flattery are exactly what an intelligence service would deploy against the most vital man in AI. Intelligence services have used romance as an opening for as long as there have been secrets worth stealing.

Industry observers note that which exposes the hidden problem of extreme wealth and power. The richer you get, the harder it becomes to know whether anyone loves you for you. Every new person in your life has a reason to be nice to you. Normal people get to skip that existential headache.

It has been revealed that money doesn't make finding love easier. Past a certain point, it makes find true love harder.

The people worth keeping are the ones who liked you before you were worth liking.

Jensen is far from the first emperor to create a commotion over love for a woman.

Paris and Helen of Troy. The Greeks' foundational story is about a prince who ran off with another man's wife and got his entire city burned to the ground. Myth, sure. But the Greeks clearly understood the risk.

It has been revealed that mark Antony and Cleopatra. Antony controlled half the Roman world. He chose Cleopatra over Rome, lost at Actium in 31 BC, and both were dead within a year. Octavian got the empire.

King Edward VIII. In 1936, he abdicated the British throne after less than a year to marry Wallis Simpson, a twice-divorced American. He traded a kingdom for love, and spent the rest of his life in comfortable, irrelevant exile.

It has been revealed that john Profumo. The closest parallel to the Jensen story. In 1963, Britain's Secretary of State for War was revealed to have had an affair with Christine Keeler, who was also involved with a Soviet naval attaché. Profumo lied to Parliament, resigned in disgrace, and the scandal helped bring down the government.

Recent findings suggest that brian Krzanich. Intel's CEO resigned in 2018 after a past consensual relationship with an employee came to light. Running a chip giant doesn't come with an exemption.

Recent findings suggest that jeff Bezos. His 2019 divorce after 25 years of marriage sent roughly 4% of Amazon, worth about $38 billion at the time, to MacKenzie Scott. Bezos kept his job, married Lauren Sánchez, and is still one of the richest men alive. But it was the most expensive breakup in history.

The pattern is clear. Kingdoms, careers, and fortunes are rebuildable. However, once you find the one, you will do anything to get them.

Remember Indecent Proposal from 1993? Robert Redford’s billionaire character offers a struggling couple, played by Demi Moore and Woody Harrelson, $1 million for one night with the wife. They take the deal. Their marriage nearly implodes.

In a recent development, the couple discovered they had a price, and it wasn’t that high. But they badly underestimated what they were selling.

Meanwhile, the billionaire could buy the night. He couldn’t buy her heart. He had everything except the one thing he actually wanted.

In a recent development, swap Redford for any modern tech billionaire and the lesson holds. Money can buy almost anything. Except the feeling of being genuinely loved.

The lack of money is a solvable problem.

Plenty of regular people have become millionaires this way. The formula is public.

There is no formula for love. You can do everything right and still never meet the one. And even if you do, roughly 40% of first marriages in America end in divorce. Finding love involves tremendous luck. Keeping it is work.

You can always make another dollar. You can't always make another soulmate.

According to recent reports, in 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General declared loneliness an epidemic. About half of American adults report feeling lonely, and the health impact of social disconnection was compared to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

The FIRE crowd isn't immune. Early retirement can be isolating. Your friends are at work. Your identity is gone. And if you're married, there's a specific trap worth sharing.

FIRE is better when both partners retire and experience freedom together. Not when one spouse is slaving away while the other is kicking back. Resentment will surely kick in.

Industry observers note that yes, I get it. Some men’s egos still need protecting when their wives are bringing home the sashimi. But men need to get over themselves. Women now make up the majority of college students, and plenty of them will out-earn their husbands.

Sources indicate that I left banking in 2012. My wife kept working until 2015 when she negotiated her own severance. For almost three years, I was the guy at home while she commuted.

If you're planning FIRE, plan a joint exit. Life is better this way.

Sources indicate that 1) A high-value spouse may need more respect just to break even. If your partner is successful, attractive, or powerful, the world is constantly praising them. Next to all that adoration, treating them normally at home can inadvertently feel like a lack of respect, or even disrespect. So you may have to deliberately show more appreciation than feels natural just to run in place.

Recent findings suggest that 2) Everything gets taken for granted. Eat Kobe beef every day and you’ll get sick of it. In FIRE land, wake up without an alarm clock every day and you’ll take that for granted too. The antidote is voluntary discomfort. Scrub your own toilets after a major investment win. Take a part-time consulting gig a 40-minute bus ride away that makes you take orders from a micromanager. Practice fasting for at least 18 hours once a month if you have access to unlimited food. Doing uncomfortable things on purpose helps you appreciate the people you already have.

3) Privacy is priceless. When you’re private, you can fix your mistakes without the whole world watching. Being known in your small circle for something good is great. Being famous means millions of strangers have opinions about who you are. Respond to all of them and you’ll never have peace of mind. Embrace being a rich nobody.

Whatever the full truth turns out to be, this whole situation is sad. Sad for Lori and their adult children. Sad for Jensen and his legacy. Disappointing for Nvidia’s tens of thousands of employees and shareholders like me. And a blow for America, given we’re in a global AI race.

Relationships are hard. They require constant work and attentiveness. Forty years of marriage doesn’t buy you immunity. If anything, it makes it easier to stop paying attention.

Sources indicate that if there’s one silver lining, it’s that this story may help bring the left and the right together on maintaining our lead in AI. AI spending has been one of the biggest drivers of U.S. economic growth. If post-midterm infighting causes us to lose the race, we could sink the economy along with it.

According to recent reports, if someone with that much money and goodwill was allegedly willing to risk throwing it away, you can’t really blame people for their emotions and their desire to be loved. We’re all human.

Besides a basic amount of financial security, I hope my kids will find someone who will support, love, and cherish them. I would rather my kids find that person than be rich.

Money can help protect them after I’m gone. But money can’t hug them after a bad day, sit with them in a hospital waiting room, or celebrate their wins with them. Knowing they each have someone like that is what will let me rest easy. That’s when I’ll know my kids will be OK.

It has been revealed that then I hope they never take that person for granted. Because the odds say they will, just like most of us take for granted the water we drink and the air we breathe.

Industry observers note that readers, do you agree that making money is easier than finding love? Would you take the $1 million in Indecent Proposal, or $2.2 million in today's dollars? If you've achieved FIRE, did you and your spouse exit together, or did one of you keep working, and how did that affect your relationship? And if you had $140+ billion, how would you ever know if someone loved you for you?

If you're a worried parent, I'm diligently working on my new book out in Fall 2027, Your Kids Will Be OK: Smart Money Decisions For Parents In An Uncertain World, published by Portfolio Penguin. It's about raising capable, resilient kids and making solid money decisions so they have a real shot at independence, and at a good life.

You can’t buy love, but you can protect it. If your family depends on your income, term life insurance is one of the most loving financial moves you can make.

It has been revealed that my wife and I each got matching 20-year term policies through Policygenius after shopping around for months. It took far less time than I expected, and we sleep better knowing our kids would be OK if the unthinkable happened. Check out Policygenius to compare quotes from top insurers for free.

It has been revealed that stocks can swing 20% on a single headline. Real estate tends to move more slowly, generate rental income, and give you something tangible to own. That’s why real estate has been a core part of my net worth for over 23 years, and it helps me sleep better when the stock market gets volatile.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan are missing on unclimbed Gangapurna West in Nepal’s Annapurna region.

Sources indicate that the Japanese pair headed to the 7,140m peak in September, and we heard no further news of them. After a major storm hit Nepal’s mountains three weeks ago, we presumed they had retreated. But now it seems they did not. They have been out of touch since October 15, after encountering severe weather conditions during their attempt to climb the peak, According to News on Nepal.

Hidesuke Taneishi, left, and Tetsu Hashimoto, right, with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

According to recent reports, the Russian team that reached the mountain earlier this month reportedly found no sign of the Japanese climbers on the peak. Bad weather forced the Russians down from their summit attempt at 6,800m.

A helicopter search-and-rescue operation is now underway, Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal has confirmed. Today, high-altitude helicopters and drones successfully recovered some of their gear, including trekking poles, near 7,050m, but the climbers themselves remain missing.

Gangapurna West is also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Make your savings goal hard to quit with a commitment device, a choice you lock in now so that backing out later takes effort or costs money. Use the least restrictive one that keeps you saving, and give the goal a dollar amount and a deadline so the device has something to hold you to.

In a recent development, you set a savings goal on a day when saving feels easy. You keep it, or don’t, on harder days, when a sale or a short paycheck makes skipping one deposit look harmless.

According to recent reports, A commitment device makes the decision for those days in advance. Ulysses had his crew tie him to the mast so he could hear the Sirens’ song without steering toward them. With money, the device removes the tempting option, or puts a price on it, before temptation arrives.

It has been revealed that economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built one into a retirement strategy. In their Save More Tomorrow program, workers agreed in advance to save part of each future raise. At the first company to offer it, participants’ average saving rate rose from 3.5% of pay to 13.6% in 40 months.

Pick a device that fits the goal:.

Sources indicate that start with the least restrictive device that keeps you saving. A penalty so steep that you hesitate to put money in leaves you saving nothing.

Give the goal an amount and a date, such as $2,400 by Oct. 1, so you and any referee know what counts as keeping it.

Set up one device this week, and keep the stricter ones for goals you’ve already broken once.

Compare the best high-yield savings accounts to choose where the goal’s money will sit.
